name: John Collison
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Stripe in 2010 at age 20 with his brother Patrick; Stripe received backing from Elon Musk, Peter Thiel, Max Levchin, and Sequoia Capital, and Collison became the world's youngest self-made billionaire by 2016 at age 25-26.
early_history_summary: Born in Limerick, Ireland to a microbiologist mother and electronic engineer father, Collison co-founded his first company 'Shuppa' with brother Patrick at age 16 in 2007. It merged with Auctomatic (Y Combinator funded) and was acquired for $5 million in March 2008 when Collison was 17. He enrolled at Harvard in 2009 but dropped out to co-found Stripe in 2010.
family_context_summary: Born to Lily (microbiologist) and Denis Collison (electronic engineer) in Limerick, Ireland. Grew up in the small village of Dromineer, County Tipperary. Middle-class professional family with strong STEM background.
parent_family_domain_summary: Mother was a microbiologist and father was an electronic engineer, providing a STEM-rich household environment. No evidence of direct business or tech-industry networks transferred from parents.
evidence_summary: Collison co-founded his first company at 16 with his brother Patrick, sold Auctomatic for $5M at 17, and co-founded Stripe at 20. His parents were both STEM professionals (microbiologist and electronic engineer). The brother partnership with Patrick was a critical complementary team advantage. Y Combinator and Silicon Valley provided the elite ecosystem network. The Auctomatic exit provided early capital and domain exposure to e-commerce/payments.

name: Eric Bina
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Bina earned his BS (1986) and MS (1988) in Computer Science from University of Illinois and joined NCSA as a programmer in 1991 at age 27. He co-created Mosaic in 1993 at age 28-29, which is his seminal achievement but falls after age 26.

name: Julian Schwinger
milestone_by_age_26: Published his first physics paper at age 16-17, completed his PhD at Columbia at 21 (1939) with a thesis on the magnetic scattering of neutrons, and was recognized by leading physicists (Rabi, Bethe, Oppenheimer) as a generational talent; by 26 he was an assistant professor at Purdue and working at MIT Radiation Lab on radar theory.
early_history_summary: Born in New York City to a garment manufacturer father, Schwinger was a precocious student who read Physical Review papers in high school. He published his first paper at 17, transferred from CCNY to Columbia via Rabi's intervention, and completed his PhD at 21. He worked at Berkeley under Oppenheimer (1939-1941), then became an instructor at Purdue (1941) before working at MIT Radiation Lab during WWII.
family_context_summary: Born to Ashkenazi Jewish parents in New York City. Father Benjamin was a garment manufacturer who emigrated from Poland. Both father and mother's parents were prosperous clothing manufacturers, though the family business declined after the 1929 Wall Street Crash. Older brother Harold was born in 1911.
parent_family_domain_summary: Family was in the garment business, not scientific. No evidence of parental scientific expertise or academic networks transferred to Julian.
evidence_summary: Schwinger was recognized as a prodigy, publishing his first physics paper at 17 and completing his PhD at 21 under Rabi at Columbia. His family was prosperous before the 1929 crash but declined afterward. Rabi was the critical mentor who recognized his talent and facilitated his transfer to Columbia. By 26, he had appointments at Berkeley, Purdue, and MIT Radiation Lab, and was recognized by the physics community as exceptional. His Nobel-winning QED work came later (1947-1948), but his early trajectory was meteoric.

name: Brian Singerman

name: Wolfgang Pauli
milestone_by_age_26: Formulated the Pauli exclusion principle in 1925 at age 24-25, a fundamental discovery in quantum mechanics stating that no two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state simultaneously. He also wrote a 237-page review of relativity theory at age 21 that Einstein praised and published as a monograph. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1945 for this discovery.
early_history_summary: Born in Vienna to a chemist father (who changed his name from Pascheles to Pauli) and a mother from a literary Jewish family, Pauli's godfather was physicist Ernst Mach. He graduated from the Döblinger-Gymnasium in 1918, published his first paper on general relativity at 18, and earned his PhD under Arnold Sommerfeld at LMU Munich in 1921 at age 21. He then worked as assistant to Max Born at Göttingen and Niels Bohr at Copenhagen before becoming a lecturer at the University of Hamburg in 1923, where he formulated the exclusion principle in 1925.
family_context_summary: Born in Vienna to Wolfgang Josef Pauli (né Pascheles), a chemist and pharmacologist, and Bertha Camilla Schütz. His godfather was the famous physicist Ernst Mach. His paternal great-grandfather was the Jewish publisher Wolf Pascheles. The family converted from Judaism to Catholicism. Pauli was raised Roman Catholic.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a scientist (chemist/pharmacologist) who published in the field. Godfather Ernst Mach was one of the most influential physicists of the era. This provided direct access to the highest levels of the physics community from childhood.
evidence_summary: Pauli was born into a scientifically connected family — his father was a chemist and his godfather was Ernst Mach. He published his first paper at 18, earned his PhD under Sommerfeld at 21, and formulated the exclusion principle at 24-25, winning the Nobel Prize in 1945. His access to the leading physics centers (Munich, Göttingen, Copenhagen) through Sommerfeld, Born, and Bohr was exceptional. Einstein praised his 237-page relativity review written at 21. The quantum mechanics revolution of the 1920s was the structural wave he rode.

The Dynabook concept was conceived in 1968, Smalltalk was developed at Xerox PARC in the 1970s, and his Turing Award came in 2003. No notable product, seminal paper, or significant discovery by age 26.

name: Guillermo Rauch
milestone_by_age_26: Created and publicly released Socket.IO in 2010 at approximately age 23-24, an influential open-source real-time communication library that became one of the most widely used web frameworks, powering products at Microsoft Office, Yammer, Zendesk, and the first Coinbase trading platform. He also co-founded LearnBoost in 2010, one of the earliest production adopters of Node.js.
early_history_summary: Born in Lanús, Buenos Aires, Argentina, Rauch grew up in a poor neighborhood with limited internet access. His father, an engineering enthusiast, brought a computer home when Guillermo was about 7. He taught himself programming, started his first business at age 11 doing remote JavaScript projects, became a core developer of the MooTools JavaScript framework at 16, and relocated to San Francisco at 18 for his first full-time engineering job. He created Socket.IO shortly after Node.js emerged in 2009, with the first commit in March 2010.
family_context_summary: Grew up in a poor area of Buenos Aires, Argentina, with limited internet access and few people having computers. His father was into engineering and Star Trek, and bought a computer for the family when Guillermo was about 7, challenging him and his brother to experiment with it. No evidence of family wealth or business networks.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father had an interest in engineering and science fiction (Star Trek), which inspired early curiosity about technology. Father actively encouraged experimentation with the family computer. No evidence of formal technical expertise or industry connections.
evidence_summary: Rauch grew up in a poor neighborhood in Argentina with limited resources, teaching himself programming from age 10 and starting a business at 11. His father's engineering enthusiasm and early computer access were catalytic. Open source communities (MooTools, then Node.js) were his primary learning and distribution channel. He became a MooTools core developer at 16, moved to SF at 18, and created Socket.IO at 23-24. The adversity of growing up in a resource-constrained environment drove him to monetize his coding skills online and seek opportunities abroad.

name: John Edensor Littlewood
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. His famous collaboration with G.H. Hardy began around 1910-1911 and their first major joint paper was published in 1914 (age 29). His early PLMS paper (1908) had limited impact. No seminal paper or significant discovery by age 26.

name: Russel Simmons
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Yelp in October 2004 at approximately age 25-26 with Jeremy Stoppelman, serving as CTO from July 2004 to June 2010. Yelp became a major public internet company (IPO 2012) and one of the leading user-generated review platforms. Prior to Yelp, Simmons was a co-founder and Lead Software Architect at PayPal.
early_history_summary: Simmons graduated from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1998 with a BS in Computer Science, and also attended the Illinois Mathematics and Science Academy (IMSA). He was a co-founder and Lead Software Architect at PayPal, where he was part of the 'PayPal Mafia.' After PayPal, he joined Max Levchin's incubator MRL Ventures, where he and Jeremy Stoppelman conceived the idea for Yelp in 2004 and co-founded the company.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Simmons attended the Illinois Mathematics and Science Academy (IMSA), a selective residential school for gifted students, suggesting early academic promise.
evidence_summary: Simmons graduated from UIUC in 1998 and became a co-founder and Lead Software Architect at PayPal, joining the influential PayPal Mafia network. Max Levchin's incubator provided the platform for the Yelp founding, and Jeremy Stoppelman was the complementary co-founder. The PayPal experience provided both financial cushioning and deep consumer internet domain exposure. IMSA attendance suggests early academic talent. Family background is not documented in reviewed sources.

name: Werner Heisenberg
milestone_by_age_26: Published the seminal Umdeutung paper in September 1925 at age 23, which established matrix mechanics and created modern quantum mechanics. Developed the uncertainty principle in 1927 at age 25-26 while working at Bohr's institute in Copenhagen. Appointed full professor at the University of Leipzig in 1927 at age 25, the youngest full professor in Germany. Received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1932 for the creation of quantum mechanics.
early_history_summary: Born in Würzburg, Germany to a secondary school teacher of classical languages who became a university professor, Heisenberg studied physics at LMU Munich under Arnold Sommerfeld (PhD 1923 at age 21) and at Göttingen under Max Born (habilitation 1924). He worked with Niels Bohr in Copenhagen (1924-1925) where he developed the ideas that led to the Umdeutung paper. After publishing matrix mechanics with Born and Pascual Jordan, he developed the uncertainty principle in 1927 and was appointed professor at Leipzig at age 25.
family_context_summary: Born to Kaspar Ernst August Heisenberg, a secondary school teacher of classical languages who became Germany's only ordentlicher Professor of medieval and modern Greek studies. Mother was Annie Wecklein. Academic family background with strong educational emphasis. Raised as a Lutheran Christian.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an academic (classical languages professor) who valued scholarship and education. The family's academic position provided access to Germany's elite educational system. No evidence of direct physics domain expertise transferred from parents.
evidence_summary: Heisenberg was the son of a university professor and had access to Germany's elite academic system. He studied under Sommerfeld (PhD at 21), Born (habilitation at 22), and Bohr (Copenhagen), the leading quantum physicists of the era. He published the seminal Umdeutung paper at 23, creating matrix mechanics with Born and Jordan, and developed the uncertainty principle at 25-26. The quantum mechanics revolution of the 1920s was the structural wave. His father's academic position provided cultural capital and educational access, though not direct physics domain knowledge.
